Below are the verse-by-verse notes for Joshua 21:23–45, drawn from the sources you specified.

---

## Joshua 21:23–26 — The Rest of the Kohathite Cities

**v. 23: “From the tribe of Dan they were given Elteke, Gibbethon…”** — These four cities from Dan had already been listed in the tribal allotment of Joshua 19:44. John Gill simply cross-references back to that earlier catalog without adding narrative comment. The Pulpit Commentary notes that for the parallel list in 1 Chronicles 6:68–70, some names differ — Kibzaim appears as Jokmeam, and Gath-rimmon (in the Manasseh verse) appears as Bileam/Ibleam, suggesting a copyist’s error where “Gath-rimmon” was inadvertently repeated from v. 24.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-21.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/joshua/21.htm

**v. 24: “Aijalon, and Gath-rimmon—four cities…”** — Aijalon was earlier listed in Joshua 19:42 and Gath-rimmon in 19:45. These were Danite towns in the southwestern coastal region. The non-priestly Kohathites thus received four cities from Dan. Bible.org’s notes observe that the tribe of Dan “had a difficult time possessing its land because of the Philistines,” and part of the tribe later migrated north (Judges 18).
- https://bible.org/seriespage/joshua-21

**v. 25: “From the half-tribe of Manasseh … Taanach and Gath-rimmon—two cities…”** — Taanach (or Tanach) was a Canaanite royal city listed among those defeated in Joshua 12:21. The Pulpit Commentary observes that “Gath-rimmon” here is almost certainly a copyist’s mistake, repeated from the previous verse. The true reading is preserved in 1 Chronicles 6:70 (Hebrew v. 56) as Ibleam (or Bileam), a Manassite town from Joshua 17:11. The Septuagint (LXX) reads “Jebath” here. Gill notes it was not unusual for cities in different tribes to share the same name.
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/joshua/21.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-21.html

**v. 26: “In all, ten cities … were given to the rest of the Kohathite clans.”** — The total: four from Ephraim (Shechem, Gezer, Kibzaim, Beth-horon), four from Dan (Elteke, Gibbethon, Aijalon, Gath-rimmon), and two from western Manasseh (Taanach, Ibleam/Gath-rimmon). These were for the non-priestly Kohathites — those who did not descend from Aaron and served as Levites rather than priests. Enduring Word notes that the Kohathites were responsible for the sanctuary furnishings (the ark, table, lampstand, altars), and their cities were in the central hill country near where the sanctuary would later be established.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-21/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-21.html

---

## Joshua 21:27–33 — The Gershonite Cities

**v. 27: “Golan in Bashan, a city of refuge for the manslayer, and Beeshterah—two cities…”** — The Gershonites, descendants of Levi’s second son, received two cities from eastern Manasseh. Golan was one of the six cities of refuge (Joshua 20:8), the northernmost on the east side of the Jordan. Beeshterah is a contraction of *Beth-Ashterah*, meaning “house/temple of Astarte.” It was the former royal city of Og, king of Bashan (called Ashtaroth in Joshua 12:4 and 1 Chronicles 6:71). Gill remarks that a temple to the goddess Astarte once stood there, but now it had become a Levitical city — a striking transformation from pagan stronghold to dwelling place for God’s ministers.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/joshua-21.html
- https://biblehub.com/commentaries/joshua/21-27.htm
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/joshua-21.html

**vv. 28–29: “From Issachar … Kishion, Daberath, Jarmuth, and En-gannim—four cities…”** — The Gershonites received four cities from Issachar. These were in the fertile Jezreel Valley region. The Preacher’s Complete Homiletical Commentary observes little is recorded in Scripture about most of these towns after this allotment; they served their purpose quietly as Levitical residences.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/joshua-21.html

**vv. 30–31: “From Asher … Mishal, Abdon, Helkath, and Rehob—four cities…”** — Four cities from the northwestern tribe of Asher. Again these are simply listed; no major biblical events are associated with them in the commentary sources reviewed.

**v. 32: “From Naphtali … Kedesh in Galilee (a city of refuge) … Hammoth-dor, and Kartan—three cities…”** — Kedesh in Galilee was the western counterpart to Golan, a city of refuge in the north. David Guzik points out that the Gershonites, whose wilderness duty was transporting the tabernacle’s coverings and curtains (Numbers 3:25–26), received cities predominantly in the northern regions of Galilee and Bashan. Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary notes Kedesh-naphtali was “one of the larger cities of the area” and “remained prominent throughout Israel’s history.”
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-21/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/joshua-21.html

**v. 33: “In all, thirteen cities … were given to the Gershonite clans.”** — The total: two from eastern Manasseh, four from Issachar, four from Asher, and three from Naphtali.

---

## Joshua 21:34–40 — The Merarite Cities

**v. 34: “This is what the Merarite clan (the rest of the Levites) were given…”** — The Merarites were responsible for transporting the tabernacle’s boards, pillars, and bases (Numbers 3:36–37). Their cities were in Zebulun (in the north), and in Reuben and Gad (east of the Jordan).

**vv. 35–37: From Zebulun, Reuben, and Gad.** — No verse-specific doctrinal commentary was found in the sources for these individual city lists. Gill and the Pulpit Commentary cross-reference the parallel list in 1 Chronicles 6:77–81, noting variant spellings (e.g., Dimnah appears as Rimmon in Chronicles). The listing follows a straightforward documentary pattern.

**v. 38: “Ramoth in Gilead, a city of refuge for the manslayer, Mahanaim…”** — Ramoth in Gilead was the third city of refuge east of the Jordan (along with Golan and Bezer). Mahanaim was the place where Jacob encountered angels (Genesis 32:2) and later served briefly as Ish-bosheth’s capital. Heshbon and Jazer were Amorite cities conquered under Moses.

**v. 39–40: “In all, twelve cities were allotted to the clans of Merari…”** — Four from Zebulun, four from Reuben, four from Gad.

---

## Joshua 21:41–42 — Summary of All Levitical Cities

**v. 41: “For the Levites … there were forty-eight cities in all…”** — This fulfills the command given through Moses in Numbers 35:7. The Levites were scattered throughout every tribe, not concentrated in one territory. David Guzik (Enduring Word) stresses this was intentional: “God wanted the Levites scattered throughout the land of Israel. He never intended there to be one state or province of Levi, but every tribe was to have the priestly influence and presence among them.” Their job included teaching the Law (Leviticus 10:11; Deuteronomy 33:10; Malachi 2:7), not just offering sacrifices.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-21/
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/joshua-21.html

**v. 42: “Each of these cities had its own surrounding pasturelands…”** — Peter Pett’s commentary explains that the “suburbs” (pasturelands) extended roughly a thousand cubits from the city walls (Numbers 35:4) and provided space for crops and animals to supplement the Levites’ food supply, which came primarily through the tithes of the people. The verse reassures readers that every single city had its pastureland — the provision was complete.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pet/joshua-21.html

---

## Joshua 21:43–45 — God’s Faithfulness: The Theological Climax

These three verses form the theological summary not only of chapters 13–21 but of the entire book of Joshua up to this point (Constable). They declare that God kept every promise — yet they must be read in tension with the reality that much land remained unconquered (Joshua 13:1–7; Judges 1:21–36).

### v. 43: “Thus the LORD gave Israel all the land He had sworn to give their fathers, and they took possession of it and settled in it.”

**Traditional reading:** God gave the land in substance; Israel had as much as they could occupy at that time. Matthew Henry writes: “Though they had often forfeited the benefit of that promise, and God had long delayed the performance of it, yet at last all difficulties were conquered, and Canaan was their own.” Enduring Word adds: “All the tribes had their land. They were still required to go into every corner of what God had given, and take full possession, but God had provided everything necessary for them to do so.” The Gibeonite deception and remaining pockets of resistance do not contradict the fact of God’s faithfulness.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/21-45.html (Henry)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-21/

### v. 44: “And the LORD gave them rest on every side … None of their enemies could stand against them…”

**Traditional reading:** “Rest” here means peace from warfare, not the absence of all Canaanites. Enduring Word notes that this marks the transition from eating the Passover “in haste” (Exodus 12:11) to eating it reclining at rest. Barnes explains: “The Canaanites were discouraged, broken in strength, holding fast in isolated spots only … The conquest of Canaan was already *ex parte Dei* [on God’s side] a perfect work.” The enemies were delivered into Israel’s hands — the rest depended on Israel’s follow-through. Constable, citing Butler, calls this “the fulfillment of God’s promise in Exodus 33:14.”
- https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/21-45.html (Barnes)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/21-45.html (Constable)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-21/

### v. 45: “Not one of all the LORD’s good promises to the house of Israel had failed; everything was fulfilled.”

**Traditional reading — universal across Protestant traditions:** This is the climactic testimony to God’s absolute covenant faithfulness. Gill says every particular “exactly, precisely, and punctually” came to pass. Matthew Henry calls it “an acquittance under their hands to the honour of God, the vindication of his promise which had been so often distrusted, and the encouragement of all believers to the end of the world.” Alexander Maclaren (Baptist preacher) described these three verses as “the trophy reared on the battlefield” — the only name on the monument is Jehovah’s.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/21-45.html (Gill)
- https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/21-45.html (Henry)
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-21/ (quoting Maclaren)

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

The traditions do not differ substantially on the meaning of the city lists (vv. 23–42), which are largely documentary. The differences emerge on **how to handle the apparent tension in vv. 43–45** between the claim that “all was fulfilled” and the fact that Canaanites remained.

**Reformed / Calvinist (Barnes, Gill, Henry, Ligonier):** God fulfilled His side of the covenant perfectly. The incomplete possession was entirely Israel’s fault — “only the inertness and pusillanimity of the Israelites … prevented the completion of the conquest” (Barnes). John Calvin stated: “Nothing but their own cowardice prevented them from enjoying the blessings of God in all their fullness.” Ligonier’s devotionals stress that “the Christian faith is founded on the promises of God” and Joshua 21:45 “encourages us that the Lord always does what He says He will do.” The promises were unconditional in God’s intent but conditional in human experience upon obedience.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/21-45.html (Barnes, quoting Calvin via Coffman)
- https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/our-promise-keeping-lord (from search excerpt)

**Dispensational (Constable):** Sees “representative universalism” at work — a Semitic literary convention where a part represents the whole. Joshua was “speaking in universal terms,” regarding the kings and areas subdued as representative of the entire land. God was faithful to promises *up to that moment*; more possession remained (Joshua 23:5), and the people needed to commit anew to the Mosaic Covenant. The promises concerning full possession were tied to Israel’s ongoing fidelity.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/21-45.html (Constable)

**Arminian / Wesleyan (Coffman, Wesley’s Notes):** Coffman (Churches of Christ, Arminian tradition) directly states: “All of God’s promises are CONTINGENT upon the obedience and cooperation of God’s children, and when that is not found, there can be no complete fulfillment of Divine promises.” Wesley’s Notes on v. 45 simply record the acknowledgment made by Joshua “in the name of all Israel.” The emphasis falls on human responsibility — what God provides must be appropriated by obedient faith.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/21-45.html (Coffman)

**Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik):** Guzik (Calvary Chapel tradition) emphasizes the application to the believer’s life: “Failure to possess what God gives is always due to His people and is never the result of His unwillingness or weakness.” He quotes Alan Redpath: “In the light of the Cross, is it not true that the enemy has no right to dwell in the land? … Is it not true that in the indwelling power of the Holy Spirit there is strength for every temptation, grace for every trial, power to overcome every difficulty?” The emphasis is on *possessing our possessions* through the Spirit’s power — a theme characteristic of Keswick / higher-life teaching.
- https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/joshua-21/

**Lutheran:** No specifically Lutheran commentary on this passage was recovered from the searched sources (lcms.org, 1517.org).

---

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship / Source Criticism (Dummelow, Peake):** Dummelow notes that Joshua 21:43–45 comes from “the later Priestly source,” while the picture of incomplete conquest in Judges comes from “an earlier document.” Peake’s Commentary is more blunt: “Both promises and performance are unhistorical. The simple fact that the descendants of Aaron could at this time have numbered only a few families shows the assignment of 13 cities to them to be purely imaginary.” In this view, the chapter is an idealized retrojection from a later period when the Levitical system was fully developed.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcb/joshua-21.html
- https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/pfc/joshua-21.html

**Catholic and Orthodox:** No commentary from Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com) or Orthodox (oca.org) sources was found in the search results for this specific passage. The available Catholic resources in the search results did not address Joshua 21:23–45 directly.

**Prosperity / Word of Faith:** No direct teaching from prosperity or Word of Faith sources on this passage was found in the searched sites. However, v. 45 (“Not one of all the LORD’s good promises … had failed”) is a text sometimes cited in popular teaching to claim that all of God’s promises — including material prosperity and physical healing — are guaranteed to every believer in this life. The traditional Protestant commentators surveyed above unanimously tie the fulfillment of God’s promises to His covenant faithfulness and ultimate redemptive purposes, not to a blanket guarantee of present material blessing. As Coffman warns, critics who say “He did not drive out all the enemies like He promised” misunderstand that the promises operate within covenant conditions.
- https://www.studylight.org/commentary/joshua/21-45.html (Coffman, for the counter-argument)
